extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; educated early-18th-century public interested in manners, morality, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic-satirical essays on manners and moral behavior in the style of The Spectator (early 18th century). They combine definitions, anecdotes, and parody to instruct and amuse a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear definitions in moral discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same Word should constantly be used in the same Sense... he earnestly recommends the use of Definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Echoing Locke: moral terms must be precisely defined to avoid confused and absurd reasoning. In moral essays, give definitions to fix meanings before arguing; failing to do so is negligent. (Context: Locke's warning about the 'Abuse of Words' and recommendation of definitions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty: The Reflection of an Ingenuous Mind, either when a Man has committed an Action for which he censures himself, or fancies that he is exposed to the Censure of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty is internal and constant (a man truly modest is as much so when alone as in company). Example: the young prince who was so moved in the Senate that he could not speak—this blush in private is praised as true modesty. Distinguish modesty from sheepishness or mere awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance: the Faculty of possessing a Man's self, or of saying and doing indifferent things without any Uneasiness or Emotion in the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assurance arises from a moderate knowledge of the world and, above all, from a mind fixed to do nothing against rules of honour and decency. An assured person, secure in his own integrity, can despise small censures from ignorance or malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the blend: Modest assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: When modesty and assurance are mixed and blended together, they compose the just Mean between Bashfulness and Impudence (a 'modest Assurance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both qualities are amiable and can coexist; the ideal character balances inward self-scrutiny (modesty) with self-possession (assurance) so one neither cringes nor is impudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and condemn the odd mixture: impudent yet bashful
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible for the same Person to be both Impudent and Bashful; frequent in people of depraved minds and mean education who cannot meet a man's eyes yet commit great villanies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern of character: superficial bashfulness masking deliberate immorality. Detecting this mixture is part of moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of virtue produces proper assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Practice of Virtue is the most proper Method to give a Man a becoming Assurance in his Words and Actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guilt seeks to shelter itself in extremes; cultivating virtue builds genuine self-possession and removes the extremes of bashfulness or impudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rest on past deeds; manage the present instant
rubrics_metrics.description: The great Rule... should be to manage the Instant in which we stand, with Fortitude, Equanimity, and Moderation; setting such a Value upon what is past as to think we have done enough is an unpardonable Folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-procrastination principle applied morally and practically: past achievements do not excuse present slackness. Use past good behavior only to inform appropriate present conduct; atoning for past faults comes by contrary behaviour, not endless self-reproach. Illustrated by Caesar's practice of continual action after victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act immediately on opportunities to do good
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can oblige any Man of Honour and Virtue? Do it immediately. Can you visit a sick Friend? Don't stay to take Coach, but be gone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral obligations and acts of charity or service should be executed without delay; deferred benevolence wastes the present and may render assistance futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership by moderation and generous policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is weakened by the full Use of it, but extended by Moderation. Give all the Men of Honour who take part with me the Terms I offered before the Battel. All my private Enemies among the Prisoners shall be spared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caesar's notes advise sustaining glory by measured action: moderation, reconciliation, and strategic generosity strengthen authority and reputation more than excess or vindictiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency and modesty in poverty; refuse dishonourable offers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Modesty usually attending faultless Poverty: reduce Manner of Living to present Circumstances rather than sollicit Friends to keep show of Estate; refuse proposals that would 'eat the Bread of Shame'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue in private hardship includes modest living and protecting family honour over immediate monetary relief obtained by dishonour. Example: Amanda's family refuses the gentleman's proposal to live with him (no marriage) despite need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of young ladies: manners, household skills, and graceful motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprint in every one an humble courteous Mind, accompanied with a graceful becoming Mein, and make them pretty much acquainted with the Houshold Part of Family-Affairs; add dancing for the beauty and spirit there is in regular Motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cultured female education (per the correspondent) combines modesty, good manners, practical household knowledge, and physical grace (dancing). Dancing is recommended to impart regular motion and to refine air and deportment (fan twirling, placing patches, tea-table behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: People follow odd fashions and leaders without knowing why
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Symbol of this Goose, you may enter into the Manner and Method of leading Creatures, with their Eyes open, thro' thick and thin, for they know not what, they know not why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory (watchman and answering goose) illustrates human susceptibility to being led by odd customs or leaders; useful as a satirical observation about herd behaviour and misplaced deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine motives of romantic passion; distinguish virtue from coquetry
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Passion proceeds from the Sense of any Virtue or Perfection in the Person beloved, I would by no means discourage it; but if ... all his heavy Complaints of Wounds and Deaths rise from some little Affectations of Coquetry... the very laying before himself the Cause of his Distemper, may be sufficient to effect the Cure of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapeutic criterion for 'dying for love': encourage love rooted in genuine virtue, but cure affectation by reflecting on motives and exposing coquetry. Practical remedy is self-examination and rational perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical technique: use of parody and comic catalogue (Bill of Mortality)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have looked over the several Bundles of letters ... and composed out of them the following Bill of Mortality ... (long list of absurd 'deaths' caused by trivial lovers' incidents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expose romantic affectation, employ parody: assemble an ironic catalogue of ludicrous 'fatal' outcomes (deadly glances, fainting at plays, being slain by a fan, etc.) to ridicule exaggerated sentimental behavior. The list-form and absurd specificity intensify the satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdotes and exempla to illustrate moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays repeatedly support abstract maxims with concrete stories: the young prince in the Senate, Caesar's tablets, Amanda's family, the watchman and goose, letters from correspondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical guideline: anchor moral argument in lively examples and narratives to make lessons memorable and persuasive. Anecdotes may also supply humorous contrast and ironic commentary.
